newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Air Force investigates rocket explosion.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Air Force investigates rocket explosion.

text.p: A sweeping investigation was underway on Saturday into the spectacular explosion of an unmanned Delta II rocket that blew up just after liftoff in a hail of flaming debris and smoke.

The U.S. Air Force named a nine-member investigative board to look into Friday's complete destruction of the $55 million McDonnell Douglas Corp. rocket and the $40 million Air Force navigational satellite it was carrying.
The board was to be headed by Col. Ron Haeke, 30th Space Wing Operations Group Commander at Vandenburg Air Force Base in California.
"It is unknown as to how long it will take to determine a cause, but the nominal time line is usually weeks to months," the Air Force said in a statement.
Air Force officials said they could offer no explanation of why the Delta II initiated its own destruction just 13 seconds after lifting off at Cape Canaveral Air Station late on Friday morning.

Speculation has centred on unusually cold weather in central Florida and the possibility of a problem with the Delta's booster rockets. On videotape, the explosion seemed to originate at the base of the Delta II, where nine solid-fuelled boosters were located, as well as the liquid-fuelled main engine.

"The first thing you're going to look at is a problem in the solid rocket motor or a problem in the guidance, navigation and control systems," said John Pike, space policy director of the American Federation of Scientists, a Washington think tank.
Pike said a problem in the rocket's on-board computers also could have caused the accident.
The debris cloud from the explosion could be seen as far as 50 miles (80 km) away, and showed up on local television station's weather radar systems.

The Air Force insisted the cloud posed a minimal health risk at worst. Most of the dangerous hydrochloric acid, hydrazine and nitrogen dioxide was either consumed in the explosion or quickly dissipated in the air, Brig. Gen. Robert Hinson, commander of the Air Force station, said after the explosion.
But there were numerous reports in the Orlando area of people who claimed ill-effects as the cloud passed over them.

"I was working outside and suddenly my hands started burning," Roy Dame, a highway construction worker said. "I went to the emergency room and they washed my hands about 10 or 11 times. I guess they're all right now."

Area hospitals reported a steady trickle of mostly eye and throat irritation complaints on Friday and a few Saturday. Most patients were treated with eyedrops or told to gargle, but none of the hospitals confirmed injuries linked to the blast.
